description: A daily noticing-and-capture habit. At the end of each day, ask 'What was the most story-worthy moment of my day? / What made today different from any other day?' and write the date plus a one-sentence summary of that five-second moment in a spreadsheet. Write a few sentences at most and never miss a day. Over weeks it installs a 'storytelling lens', surfaces dozens of overlooked daily moments, and builds a treasury of hundreds of story seeds; Dicks claims it also slows down time and makes life feel more vivid.

Set a timer (10 min; ideally 15 min daily) and write continuously, 'dreaming with the tip of your pen.' Three rules: (1) do not attach to any one idea, (2) do not judge any thought, no matter how strange/vulgar/disturbing, ignore grammar and penmanship, (3) never let the pen stop moving -- when stuck, fall back to listing colors, numbers (in words), or countries until a new thought appears. Afterward, review the page and harvest story ideas, anecdotes, phrases, and memories.

Make a table with a Prompt column and First / Last / Best / Worst columns. Fill the prompts with everyday categories (kiss, car, job, teacher, pet, gift, trouble, injury, meal, vacation...). For each prompt, recall your first, last, best, and worst instance and jot a short memory reminder (not the full story yet). Review to find emotionally rich or surprising memories; entries that recur are strong story candidates. Doubles as a conversation game for first dates, interviews, and car rides.

A game-based story-finding method from the Storyworthy Moments course that turns random memories into structured story ideas. Reconstructed mechanic: use a small countdown of prompts to rapidly surface and then shape raw memories into a usable seed. Confirmed as a named module; exact step procedure is paywalled.

A story-finding drill that leverages physical locations and places as emotional triggers: walk through specific settings from your life (a childhood home, a school, a workplace, a hospital) and let each location surface the memories and moments attached to it. Confirmed as a named Storyworthy Moments module; exact steps are paywalled.

A story-finding drill that mines universal stories from moments involving loss and rediscovery -- things, people, beliefs, or opportunities you lost and/or found again. Confirmed as a named Storyworthy Moments module; exact steps are paywalled.

Before drafting, identify the single five-second moment of transformation your story is really about -- the instant something fundamentally changed (you fell in/out of love, changed your mind, forgave, despaired, realized something). The story must show you 'walked in as one person and walked out as another.' Every other element exists only to set up that moment; a story can never be about two things.

exercise_name: Start at the Opposite / End on the Heart
description: Structuring drill: your ending is the five-second moment of transformation, so make your beginning the OPPOSITE state. Use 'I once was X but now I am Y' -- if the moment is hopeful, open in despair. Start as close to the end as possible, open with movement/action (no preamble or summary), and always end on the emotional heart, never on a laugh. Fight for your beginnings; first ideas are rarely best.

Revision drill: go through your story and replace 'and then' connections between events with 'but' and 'therefore' (explicitly or implicitly -- also so / because / instead / as a result). Scenes joined by 'and then' have no momentum; causation creates change and forward motion. Borrows the South Park rule: if 'and then' fits between scenes, the story is stuck.

exercise_name: Movie in the Mind (set every scene)
description: Craft drill: attach a physical location to every moment of the story so the audience can run a 'movie in their minds.' Every moment should be a scene and every scene needs a setting; if the audience always knows where you are, the film keeps running. Think like a film director -- give visual anchors, avoid thesis statements and exposition breaks.

Authenticity check: ask 'Would I tell this story this way to a friend at dinner?' If not, you're telling it wrong. No purple prose, no invented dialogue, no theatrical hand movements -- keep it first-person, vulnerable, conversational, told from your perspective of how it affected you. Also a filter for whether a moment is even worth telling.

Stakes device: within the first ~30 seconds, state a clear, large, obvious need / want / problem / peril / mystery -- 'the thing everyone in the room can see.' It signals that a story (not a musing) is starting and gives the audience a reason to listen and wonder, infusing instant stakes. Drill: rewrite your opening so it raises an immediate question (e.g. 'When I was nine, I wanted to disown my mother' rather than 'My mother was perfect'). The Elephant can also 'change colors' mid-story.

Stakes device: just before a key event, load the audience with all of your hopes and fears in that moment -- 'turn your plan into their plan' -- so they share your anticipation and feel the same emotion you felt. Most powerful when the plan then fails, because the struggle and disappointment land on them too. Drill: insert a beat that voices your in-the-moment hopes/fears before moving the story forward.

Suspense device: hint at a coming event but reveal just enough to keep the audience guessing without letting them predict correctly. Especially effective when the truly unexpected is coming. Drill: plant a small unexplained detail early (e.g. mention a crumpled fast-food uniform exists) and withhold its purpose until later.

Suspense device: at the moment the audience is hanging on your every word near the payoff, deliberately slow down or stop the story cold. Drag out the wait by describing things that don't strictly need describing (the house, a uniform, an old man's face), using words that suggest stakes/danger, to maximize anticipation before the reveal. Drill: find your climax, then insert deliberate slow-down detail right before it.

Suspense device: make a plausible FALSE prediction about your immediate future in the story (e.g. 'I was sure the police were about to arrest me'), so the audience -- who are 'prediction machines' -- wonder whether it will come true. Deploy only when the guess seems reasonable and presents an intriguing possibility. Drill: voice an in-the-moment expectation that the story will then subvert.

Surprise technique: the only way to make an audience cry is to surprise them, so hide the critical information until the reveal. Three methods: (1) bury the key detail in clutter among irrelevant details, (2) place it far in distance from its payoff so its significance isn't recognized, (3) camouflage it with laughter so the audience assumes you were just being funny. Drill: identify your story's key fact and deliberately obscure it using one of the three methods.

Surprise technique: maximize the contrast between the surprise moment and the moment immediately before it (a peaceful day before the crash; parents checking the car before checking on their son; a crowded waiting room against a theme of isolation). 'Contrast is king', and laughter can provide contrast to something authentically awful. Drill: sharpen the before-moment so the turn hits harder.

Humor strategy: push together two things that rarely or never go together to create comic incongruity (the 'baby' and the 'blender'). The unexpected juxtaposition generates the laugh. Drill: take an element of your story and pair it with something absurdly mismatched.

Humor structure modeled on the carnival game: the stacked milk cans are your SETUP and the baseball is your PUNCHLINE. Build the tower with careful language that raises anticipation and save the funniest word/idea for LAST (the throw). The more milk cans you stack (the bigger the setup), the greater the potential laugh; the better you deliver the final word, the more of that potential you realize. Drill: reorder a funny line so the funniest word lands at the very end.

Humor strategy: define an object, person, or idea in its most basic essence, choosing only the aspects that are surprising, amusing, or traditionally left unspoken (e.g. reframing a Christmas tree, stockings, or Elf on a Shelf in blunt essential terms). Drill: pick something familiar in your story and write a one-line stripped-down definition that exposes its absurd essence.

Humor-timing principle: get the audience to laugh within the first 30 seconds, and always make people laugh BEFORE you make them cry ('it hurts more that way'). Use laughter to reset tension when a story gets too tense and to camouflage important information. Drill: place an early laugh near the opening and a laugh just before your emotional turn.

Phrasing technique: say what something or someone is NOT rather than what it is -- it almost always lands harder and carries an implied 'but'. Example: 'I'm not smart, I'm not good-looking, and no one likes me' beats the positive framing. Drill: rewrite a flat descriptive line in your story as a negation.

Truth-shaping pass: reshape a true story for the audience's benefit (never to invent what didn't happen) using five moves -- Omission (cut details/people that don't serve the five-second moment), Compression (push time/space together; 'years are boring, days are thrilling'), Assumption (make reasonable guesses about forgotten details you need), Progression (reorder events for emotional payoff rather than chronology), and Conflation (compress a long intellectual/emotional change into a single moment). Drill: apply each lie to a draft to tighten and sharpen it.

Scoping technique: big stories fail because they're unrelatable, so find the small, relatable, comprehensible moments inside larger ones -- 'the little moments hidden inside big moments' (friends in the waiting room, not the car crash itself). The universal small moment is what creates connection. Drill: take a big dramatic event and locate the tiny human moment to actually tell.

Rehearsal/delivery method: do NOT memorize a story word-for-word. Memorize only (1) your first few sentences, (2) your final sentences, and (3) the sequence of scenes. This gives structure while keeping delivery natural and varied. Drill: rehearse a story holding only the opening lines, closing lines, and the ordered list of scenes.

exercise_name: Delivery Rules (no questions, no props, three faces)
description: Performance constraints to drill while telling: no rhetorical questions (they turn storytelling into Q&A), no props (they always hurt), never address the audience or say the word 'story' inside the story, always use a mic and speak to the back of the room, and find three smiling/nodding people (left, center, right) to use as emotional guideposts. Manage your emotions rather than performing them; a little nervousness is endearing.

exercise_name: Practice Your Stories (live workshop telling + feedback)
description: The live-workshop and community practice format: bring a found story, tell it aloud to the group/mentor, and receive supportive group coaching and feedback, iterating toward 2-3 polished, ready-to-tell stories. Run in Matthew's 6-hour live workshop (three 2-hour sessions) and in the recurring community 'Practice Your Stories' sessions.
